sets.title: Catalysis vocabulary
sets.unlock_rule: Schedule only after every associated knowledge record has been encountered in a completed or in-progress Unit 3 story.

questions.prompt: This is the initial energy barrier reactants must overcome to reach the transition state.
questions.explanation: Activation energy is the initial energy barrier that reactants must overcome to reach the transition state of a reaction.

questions.prompt: This protein functions as a biological catalyst in cells.
questions.explanation: Enzymes are proteins that function as biological catalysts in cells.

questions.prompt: This is the reactant molecule on which a catalyst acts.
questions.explanation: A substrate is a reactant molecule on which an enzyme acts.

questions.prompt: This is the region of a catalyst where a compatible reactant binds and catalysis occurs.
questions.explanation: The active site is the region of an enzyme where compatible substrate binds and catalysis occurs.

questions.prompt: This temporary bound state exists after the reactant has docked at the catalyst before products are released.
questions.explanation: The enzyme-substrate complex model represents substrate binding at the active site.

sets.title: Active-site models
sets.unlock_rule: Schedule only after every associated knowledge record has been encountered in a completed or in-progress Unit 3 story.

questions.prompt: This describes the requirement that reactant shape and charge fit the catalytic binding region.
questions.explanation: For an enzyme-mediated reaction to occur, substrate shape and charge must be compatible with the enzyme active site.

questions.prompt: This is the conformational change triggered by binding that improves catalytic interactions.
questions.explanation: Induced fit is a change in enzyme conformation triggered by substrate binding that improves catalytic interactions in the active site.

sets.title: Enzyme disruption mechanisms
sets.unlock_rule: Schedule only after every associated knowledge record has been encountered in a completed or in-progress Unit 3 story.

questions.prompt: This is loss of functional protein structure caused by disruptive temperature, pH, or chemical conditions.
questions.explanation: Temperature, pH, or chemical-environment changes can disrupt enzyme protein structure and eliminate catalytic ability.

questions.prompt: This describes structural disruption from which catalytic activity can return when conditions are restored.
questions.explanation: In some cases enzyme denaturation is reversible and activity can return when conditions are restored.

questions.prompt: This occurs when an inhibitor forms a persistent, often covalent interaction that inactivates the catalyst.
questions.explanation: Irreversible inhibitors form very stable interactions, often covalent, that persistently inactivate an enzyme; this is distinct from the standard reversible competitive-inhibition model.

sets.title: Inhibition mechanisms
sets.unlock_rule: Schedule only after every associated knowledge record has been encountered in a completed or in-progress Unit 3 story.

questions.prompt: This inhibition occurs when a reversible inhibitor occupies the catalytic binding region and reduces reactant access.
questions.explanation: Competitive inhibitors can bind reversibly to an enzyme active site and reduce substrate access.

questions.prompt: This inhibition occurs when binding at a regulatory site away from the catalytic site decreases activity.
questions.explanation: Noncompetitive inhibitors can bind allosteric sites and change enzyme activity.

questions.prompt: This occurs when an inhibitor forms a persistent, often covalent interaction that inactivates the catalyst.
questions.explanation: Irreversible inhibitors form very stable interactions, often covalent, that persistently inactivate an enzyme; this is distinct from the standard reversible competitive-inhibition model.

sets.title: Enzyme helpers
sets.unlock_rule: Schedule only after every associated knowledge record has been encountered in a completed or in-progress Unit 3 story.

questions.prompt: This is a nonprotein helper required by some catalysts and can include an inorganic metal ion.
questions.explanation: A cofactor is a nonprotein helper required for the function of some enzymes; inorganic cofactors can include metal ions.

questions.prompt: This is an organic helper, often derived from a vitamin.
questions.explanation: A coenzyme is an organic cofactor; many coenzymes are derived from vitamins.

questions.prompt: This is the catalytically active enzyme complex with its required helper or helpers associated.
questions.explanation: A holoenzyme is the catalytically active enzyme complex with its required cofactor or cofactors associated.

sets.title: Allosteric control
sets.unlock_rule: Schedule only after every associated knowledge record has been encountered in a completed or in-progress Unit 3 story.

questions.prompt: This is a regulatory binding location distinct from the catalytic binding region.
questions.explanation: An allosteric site is a regulatory binding site distinct from an enzyme’s active site.

questions.prompt: This regulatory molecule binds away from the catalytic site and stabilizes a more active conformation.
questions.explanation: An allosteric activator is a regulatory molecule that binds an allosteric site and stabilizes a more active enzyme conformation.

questions.prompt: This regulatory molecule binds away from the catalytic site and stabilizes a less active conformation.
questions.explanation: An allosteric inhibitor is a regulatory molecule that binds an allosteric site and stabilizes a less active enzyme conformation.

sets.title: Pathway regulation
sets.unlock_rule: Schedule only after every associated knowledge record has been encountered in a completed or in-progress Unit 3 story.

questions.prompt: This occurs when binding at one site of a multisubunit enzyme increases activity at additional sites.
questions.explanation: Cooperativity occurs in some multisubunit enzymes when substrate binding at one active site promotes a conformation that increases activity at other active sites.

questions.prompt: This occurs when a downstream product inhibits an earlier enzyme in the same pathway.
questions.explanation: Feedback inhibition occurs when a downstream product inhibits an enzyme acting earlier in the same metabolic pathway, reducing further product formation.

questions.prompt: This general control mechanism changes enzyme activity through noncovalent regulatory binding away from the active site.
questions.explanation: Allosteric regulation occurs when a regulatory molecule binds noncovalently at a site other than the active site and changes enzyme activity through a conformational change.

sets.title: Metabolic direction
sets.unlock_rule: Schedule only after every associated knowledge record has been encountered in a completed or in-progress Unit 3 story.

questions.prompt: This pathway breaks complex molecules into simpler products and typically releases usable energy.
questions.explanation: Catabolic pathways break complex molecules into simpler products and typically release usable energy.

questions.prompt: This pathway builds complex molecules from simpler components and requires energy input.
questions.explanation: Anabolic pathways build complex molecules from simpler components and require energy input.

sets.title: Energy forms
sets.unlock_rule: Schedule only after every associated knowledge record has been encountered in a completed or in-progress Unit 3 story.

questions.prompt: This is energy associated with directed or observable motion.
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy is energy associated with motion.

questions.prompt: This is kinetic energy associated with random molecular motion.
questions.explanation: Thermal energy is kinetic energy associated with random movement of atoms and molecules.

questions.prompt: This is stored energy associated with position or structure.
questions.explanation: Potential energy is stored energy associated with position or structure.

questions.prompt: This is stored molecular energy that can be transformed during reactions.
questions.explanation: Chemical energy is potential energy associated with molecular structure that can be transformed during chemical reactions.

sets.title: Thermodynamic laws
sets.unlock_rule: Schedule only after every associated knowledge record has been encountered in a completed or in-progress Unit 3 story.

questions.prompt: This law states that energy is transferred or transformed but is not created or destroyed.
questions.explanation: Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can be transferred or transformed.

questions.prompt: This law states that energy transformations increase total entropy and disperse some energy as less-useful heat.
questions.explanation: Every energy transfer or transformation increases the entropy of the universe, and some energy becomes less available to perform work, often dispersing as heat.

sets.title: Reaction energetics
sets.unlock_rule: Schedule only after every associated knowledge record has been encountered in a completed or in-progress Unit 3 story.

questions.prompt: This reaction has a negative free-energy change and is thermodynamically spontaneous even if it may proceed slowly.
questions.explanation: An exergonic reaction has a negative change in free energy and can proceed spontaneously in the thermodynamic sense; spontaneity does not imply a fast rate.

questions.prompt: This reaction has a positive free-energy change and must be coupled to an energy-releasing process in cells.
questions.explanation: An endergonic reaction has a positive change in free energy and requires coupling to an energy-releasing process to proceed in cells.

sets.title: Cellular work
sets.unlock_rule: Schedule only after every associated knowledge record has been encountered in a completed or in-progress Unit 3 story.

questions.prompt: This category includes muscle contraction, ciliary movement, and chromosome movement.
questions.explanation: Mechanical work includes processes such as ciliary movement, chromosome movement, and muscle contraction.

questions.prompt: This category moves substances across membranes against thermodynamically favored directions.
questions.explanation: Transport work moves substances across membranes against thermodynamically favored directions.

questions.prompt: This category drives endergonic synthesis such as building polymers from monomers.
questions.explanation: Chemical work drives endergonic reactions such as synthesis of polymers from monomers.

sets.title: ATP coupling
sets.unlock_rule: Schedule only after every associated knowledge record has been encountered in a completed or in-progress Unit 3 story.

questions.prompt: This reaction converts ATP and water to ADP and inorganic phosphate with a negative free-energy change under cellular conditions.
questions.explanation: ATP hydrolysis converts ATP and water to ADP and inorganic phosphate and has a negative free-energy change under cellular conditions.

questions.prompt: This is transfer or addition of a phosphate group to a molecule, often changing its reactivity or conformation.
questions.explanation: Phosphorylation is transfer or addition of a phosphate group to a molecule; ATP-driven phosphorylation can alter a molecule’s reactivity, free energy, or protein conformation.

questions.prompt: This continuously reforms ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate using energy from exergonic processes.
questions.explanation: ATP is continually regenerated from ADP and inorganic phosphate using energy released by exergonic processes.

sets.title: Carbon acquisition
sets.unlock_rule: Schedule only after every associated knowledge record has been encountered in a completed or in-progress Unit 3 story.

questions.prompt: This organismal strategy builds organic molecules from inorganic carbon using light or chemical energy.
questions.explanation: An autotroph builds organic molecules from inorganic carbon such as CO2 using energy from light or chemical reactions.

questions.prompt: This carbon-acquisition strategy uses light energy to build organic molecules from inorganic carbon.
questions.explanation: A photoautotroph uses light energy to build organic molecules from inorganic carbon.

questions.prompt: This strategy obtains organic carbon from preexisting organic molecules made by other organisms.
questions.explanation: A heterotroph obtains organic carbon from preexisting organic molecules made by other organisms.

sets.title: Chloroplast locations
sets.unlock_rule: Schedule only after every associated knowledge record has been encountered in a completed or in-progress Unit 3 story.

questions.prompt: This chloroplast fluid compartment lies outside the thylakoids and contains Calvin-cycle reactions.
questions.explanation: The stroma is the fluid inside the inner chloroplast membrane and outside the thylakoids; Calvin-cycle carbon-fixation reactions occur there.

questions.prompt: This chloroplast membrane contains photosystems, pigments, electron-transfer components, and ATP synthase.
questions.explanation: Thylakoid membranes contain chlorophyll organized into photosystems together with electron-transport proteins.

questions.prompt: This is a stack of thylakoids.
questions.explanation: Thylakoids form stacks called grana, and the light reactions occur on thylakoid membranes in these stacks.

sets.title: Photosynthetic pigments
sets.unlock_rule: Schedule only after every associated knowledge record has been encountered in a completed or in-progress Unit 3 story.

questions.prompt: This is the primary reaction-center pigment in oxygenic photosynthesis.
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll a is the primary reaction-center pigment in oxygenic photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: This accessory pigment broadens the wavelengths usable for photosynthesis in plants and green algae.
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll b is an accessory chlorophyll that broadens the wavelengths usable for photosynthesis in plants and green algae.

questions.prompt: These accessory pigments broaden absorption and help dissipate excess excitation energy.
questions.explanation: Carotenoids are accessory pigments that broaden light absorption and can dissipate excess light energy, helping protect the photosynthetic apparatus.

sets.title: Photosystem components
sets.unlock_rule: Schedule only after every associated knowledge record has been encountered in a completed or in-progress Unit 3 story.

questions.prompt: This thylakoid complex contains both a reaction center and surrounding light-harvesting pigments/proteins.
questions.explanation: A photosystem is a thylakoid-membrane complex containing a reaction center and surrounding light-harvesting pigments and proteins.

questions.prompt: This pigment-protein assembly transfers excitation energy toward a reaction center.
questions.explanation: Light-harvesting complexes contain pigment molecules bound to proteins and transfer excitation energy toward the reaction center.

questions.prompt: This part contains a special chlorophyll pair and primary electron acceptor where excitation becomes electron transfer.
questions.explanation: A photosystem reaction center contains a special chlorophyll pair and primary electron acceptor where excitation leads to electron transfer.

sets.title: Photosystems
sets.unlock_rule: Schedule only after every associated knowledge record has been encountered in a completed or in-progress Unit 3 story.

questions.prompt: This light-driven complex receives replacement electrons from water oxidation after transferring an excited electron.
questions.explanation: Photosystem II absorbs light, transfers an excited electron to an acceptor, and receives replacement electrons from water oxidation.

questions.prompt: This light-driven complex re-excites arriving electrons and supports reduction of NADP+.
questions.explanation: Photosystem I re-excites electrons arriving from the thylakoid electron transport chain and supports reduction of NADP+ to NADPH.

sets.title: Light-reaction energy products
sets.unlock_rule: Schedule only after every associated knowledge record has been encountered in a completed or in-progress Unit 3 story.

questions.prompt: This light-reaction product supplies chemical energy for Calvin-cycle work.
questions.explanation: The light reactions capture light energy to produce ATP and NADPH, which provide energy and reducing power for carbohydrate production in the Calvin cycle.

questions.prompt: This reduced electron carrier supplies reducing power for Calvin-cycle carbon reduction.
questions.explanation: In photosynthesis, electrons passing through the thylakoid electron transport system ultimately reduce NADP+ to NADPH in association with photosystem I.

sets.title: Photosynthetic phases
sets.unlock_rule: Schedule only after every associated knowledge record has been encountered in a completed or in-progress Unit 3 story.

questions.prompt: This photosynthetic phase captures light energy and produces ATP and reducing power on thylakoid membranes.
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis can be organized into light reactions that capture light energy and a Calvin cycle that uses ATP and NADPH to reduce carbon dioxide to carbohydrate.

questions.prompt: This cyclic stromal pathway uses ATP and reducing power to incorporate CO2 into carbohydrate.
questions.explanation: The Calvin cycle is a cyclic carbon-fixation pathway in the chloroplast stroma that uses ATP and NADPH to incorporate CO2 into carbohydrate.

sets.title: Calvin-cycle roles
sets.unlock_rule: Schedule only after every associated knowledge record has been encountered in a completed or in-progress Unit 3 story.

questions.prompt: This enzyme catalyzes initial CO2 fixation and can also react with O2.
questions.explanation: Rubisco is the enzyme that catalyzes the initial CO2-fixation reaction of the Calvin cycle and can also react with O2.

questions.prompt: This five-carbon CO2 acceptor is regenerated so the carbon-fixation cycle can continue.
questions.explanation: Ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP) is the CO2-acceptor molecule regenerated in the Calvin cycle.

questions.prompt: This three-carbon sugar product can leave the cycle and contribute to glucose and other organic molecules.
questions.explanation: Glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate (G3P) is a three-carbon sugar produced by the Calvin cycle and can be used to synthesize glucose and other organic molecules.

sets.title: Carbon-conservation strategies
sets.unlock_rule: Schedule only after every associated knowledge record has been encountered in a completed or in-progress Unit 3 story.

questions.prompt: This process begins when the carbon-fixing enzyme reacts with O2, lowering net carbon fixation.
questions.explanation: Photorespiration occurs when rubisco reacts with O2 instead of CO2, consuming energy and lowering net carbon fixation; it is favored when internal CO2 is low relative to O2.

questions.prompt: This adaptation reduces photorespiration by initially fixing carbon in mesophyll cells and delivering CO2 to bundle-sheath cells.
questions.explanation: C4 plants initially fix CO2 into four-carbon compounds in mesophyll cells and deliver concentrated CO2 to bundle-sheath cells, reducing photorespiration through spatial separation.

questions.prompt: This adaptation reduces water loss by taking in CO2 mainly at night and releasing stored CO2 during the day.
questions.explanation: CAM plants open stomata mainly at night, store fixed carbon in organic acids, and release CO2 during the day for the Calvin cycle, reducing water loss through temporal separation.

sets.title: Respiratory electron carriers
sets.unlock_rule: Schedule only after every associated knowledge record has been encountered in a completed or in-progress Unit 3 story.

questions.prompt: This oxidized/reduced carrier pair accepts electrons during fuel oxidation and delivers them to the respiratory ETC.
questions.explanation: NAD+ accepts electrons and a proton to become NADH; NADH carries high-energy electrons to other reactions including the respiratory electron transport chain.

questions.prompt: This carrier pair is reduced during the citric acid cycle and feeds electrons into the respiratory ETC at a different entry point.
questions.explanation: FAD accepts electrons and protons during the citric acid cycle to become FADH2, which can deliver electrons to the respiratory electron transport chain.

sets.title: Phosphorylation mechanisms
sets.unlock_rule: Schedule only after every associated knowledge record has been encountered in a completed or in-progress Unit 3 story.

questions.prompt: This ATP-forming mechanism directly transfers a phosphate from an organic substrate to ADP.
questions.explanation: Substrate-level phosphorylation forms ATP by direct enzymatic transfer of a phosphate group from an organic substrate to ADP.

questions.prompt: This respiratory ATP-forming mechanism couples electron transport, a proton gradient, chemiosmosis, and ATP synthase.
questions.explanation: Protons flow through ATP synthase by chemiosmosis to drive ATP formation; in aerobic respiration this process is oxidative phosphorylation.

questions.prompt: This photosynthetic ATP-forming mechanism uses a light-generated proton gradient and ATP synthase.
questions.explanation: Protons flow through membrane-bound ATP synthase by chemiosmosis, driving ATP formation from ADP and inorganic phosphate; in photosynthesis this is photophosphorylation.

sets.title: Respiration stages
sets.unlock_rule: Schedule only after every associated knowledge record has been encountered in a completed or in-progress Unit 3 story.

questions.prompt: This cytosolic stage splits one six-carbon glucose into two three-carbon pyruvate molecules.
questions.explanation: Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol and splits one six-carbon glucose into two three-carbon pyruvate molecules.

questions.prompt: This stage converts mitochondrial pyruvate to an acetyl group carried by coenzyme A while producing CO2 and NADH.
questions.explanation: During standard aerobic eukaryotic respiration, pyruvate is transported into mitochondria and oxidized to an acetyl group carried by coenzyme A, producing CO2 and NADH.

questions.prompt: This cyclic matrix pathway oxidizes acetyl groups, releases CO2, and reduces NAD+ and FAD.
questions.explanation: The citric acid cycle, also called the Krebs cycle, oxidizes acetyl groups in the mitochondrial matrix and transfers energy to ATP, NADH, and FADH2 while releasing CO2.

questions.prompt: This stage combines respiratory electron transport that builds a proton gradient with chemiosmosis through ATP synthase.
questions.explanation: Oxidative phosphorylation includes electron transport that establishes a proton gradient and chemiosmosis through ATP synthase.

sets.title: Respiratory gradient locations
sets.unlock_rule: Schedule only after every associated knowledge record has been encountered in a completed or in-progress Unit 3 story.

questions.prompt: This mitochondrial compartment lies inside the inner membrane and contains pyruvate-oxidation and citric-cycle machinery.
questions.explanation: Eukaryotic aerobic respiration uses mitochondrial compartments including the matrix, inner membrane, cristae, and intermembrane space.

questions.prompt: This mitochondrial compartment accumulates a higher proton concentration than the matrix during respiratory electron transport.
questions.explanation: Electron transfer through the respiratory electron transport chain is coupled to formation of a proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane, with higher proton concentration in the intermembrane space than in the matrix.

sets.title: Energy-harvesting alternatives
sets.unlock_rule: Schedule only after every associated knowledge record has been encountered in a completed or in-progress Unit 3 story.

questions.prompt: This energy-harvesting route uses an ETC and oxygen as terminal electron acceptor in its standard oxygen-dependent form.
questions.explanation: Aerobic cellular respiration in eukaryotes uses coordinated enzyme-catalyzed reactions to capture energy from biological macromolecules.

questions.prompt: This energy-harvesting route still uses an ETC but ends with a terminal electron acceptor other than oxygen.
questions.explanation: Anaerobic respiration uses an electron transport chain with a terminal electron acceptor other than oxygen.

questions.prompt: This route regenerates NAD+ without an ETC so glycolysis can continue when oxidative reoxidation is limited.
questions.explanation: Fermentation regenerates NAD+ without an electron transport chain so glycolysis can continue when oxidative NADH reoxidation cannot meet demand.

sets.title: Fermentation products
sets.unlock_rule: Schedule only after every associated knowledge record has been encountered in a completed or in-progress Unit 3 story.

questions.prompt: This pathway converts pyruvate to acetaldehyde, releases CO2, then produces ethanol while regenerating NAD+.
questions.explanation: Alcohol fermentation converts pyruvate to ethanol and CO2 while oxidizing NADH to regenerate NAD+.

questions.prompt: This pathway reduces pyruvate directly to lactate while regenerating NAD+ and releasing no CO2 in the conversion.
questions.explanation: In lactate-producing fermentation, pyruvate is reduced by NADH to lactate, regenerating NAD+.
